chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi narrated to us, from his father, from his grandfather Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, who linked it up to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), who said:
Ten parts of a dead corpse are clean (pure): the bones, the hair, the wool, the feathers, the horn, the hoof, the eggs, the breast (or udder), the milk, and the teeth.

key_terms.الْمَيْتَة: Carcass or dead animal (specifically one not slaughtered ritually)

ai.seo_question: Which parts of a dead animal are considered ritually pure in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Kisāl* highlights the distinct Shia jurisprudential view that ten specific parts of an animal—such as bones, hair, and milk—remain ritually pure (tahir) even if the animal was not slaughtered according to Islamic rites, distinguishing them from the flesh. This enumeration underscores the principle that certain bodily excretions and structural components are inherently clean, a point of discussion among jurists regarding the scope of *maytah* (carcass) impurity. The list serves as a practical guide for daily purity, clarifying that items like wool and feathers do not require the animal to be ritually slaughtered to be considered pure.
